slides.title: 01 // PROBLEM STATEMENT: Stateful Protocol Vulnerabilities

presenter.name: Tanmay
presenter.topic: Project Overview, Threat Landscape, Paradigm Shift & Research Scope

slides.spokenScript: To understand why automata theory is indispensable, we must examine how modern communication protocols actually function. Protocols such as HTTP, TLS, and SSH are fundamentally stateful systems: actions are only valid when executed in a strict, pre-defined sequential order. Traditional signature-based firewalls inspect payload strings, while contemporary machine learning models compute statistical likelihoods. Crucially, neither approach mathematically verifies whether an observed sequence of protocol transitions is legal according to specification. Attackers exploit this blind spot in three primary ways: First, Out-of-Order Execution—where a server response is emitted before any client request is received. Second, Authentication Bypass—where an adversary accesses protected resources without traversing the required authentication state. And third, Session Confusion—where packets are injected into terminated or half-open connections. These are not payload anomalies—they are structural protocol invariant violations.

slides.title: 02 // PARADIGM SHIFT: Black-Box ML vs. Formal Automata

presenter.name: Tanmay
presenter.topic: Project Overview, Threat Landscape, Paradigm Shift & Research Scope

slides.spokenScript: This slide captures the fundamental paradigm shift at the heart of TraceGuard AI. When organizations rely solely on black-box statistical machine learning for protocol security, they encounter three severe theoretical and operational hurdles: First, High False Positives: unusual, rare, but perfectly legitimate protocol sequences are misclassified as anomalies. Second, Zero Formal Proof: deep neural networks output probability values without a causal chain explaining why a sequence violates protocol grammar. And third, Inference Latency: evaluating complex feature matrices introduces packet-processing lag that cannot sustain line-rate network speeds. In contrast, our formal Automata Theory approach provides: Constant O(1) step decisions—each packet triggers an instantaneous table lookup; zero false positives on specification-compliant grammar; and total explainability—pinpointing the exact state-symbol transition that caused a violation.

slides.title: 04 // REGULAR LANGUAGE THEORY: Regular Languages & Kleene's Law

presenter.name: Karthik Sai
presenter.topic: Chomsky Hierarchy, Kleene's Law, Total Completeness & 5-Tuple Definition

slides.spokenScript: In formal language theory, Type-3 regular grammars occupy the foundational tier of the Chomsky hierarchy. By Kleene's Theorem, regular languages are precisely those recognized by finite-state automata. Why is this theorem critical for high-speed network security? First, a Deterministic Finite Automaton possesses the memoryless state property: each state transition depends strictly and exclusively on the current active state q and the next incoming event symbol σ. It requires no auxiliary tape and no unbounded stack. Second, language membership is decidable in strict linear time O(|w|), where |w| represents the number of observed packets in a session trace. While higher-level grammars like Pushdown Automata or Turing Machines offer greater expressive power, their parsing algorithms introduce super-linear complexity or undecidability. Type-3 DFAs provide the exact mathematical sweet spot: sufficient expressiveness to validate protocol ordering, with guaranteed line-rate execution.

slides.title: 05 // MATHEMATICAL COMPLETENESS: Total Transition Completeness

presenter.name: Karthik Sai
presenter.topic: Chomsky Hierarchy, Kleene's Law, Total Completeness & 5-Tuple Definition

slides.spokenScript: This slide represents our primary mathematical invariant: Total Transition Function Completeness. In many textbook automata and informal implementations, transition functions are left partial: if an unexpected event arrives, the automaton simply lacks a transition arrow. In cybersecurity, an undefined transition is a fatal vulnerability—it leads to unhandled exceptions, undefined behavior, or silent bypasses. In TraceGuard AI, we formally enforce that δ is a total function: For all states q in Q, and for all alphabet symbols σ in Σ, δ(q, σ) maps deterministically to a well-defined state in Q. With 9 states and 13 discrete alphabet symbols, our state transition matrix contains exactly 9 times 13 equals 117 fully defined cells, leaving zero mathematical loopholes.
slides.slideNotes: Details total function invariant: 9 states x 13 symbols = 117 defined cells. Formal theorem: ∀q ∈ Q, ∀σ ∈ Σ, δ(q, σ) ∈ Q. Eliminates unhandled state exceptions.

9 states × 13 event symbols = 117 fully mapped transitions

defenseQuestions.question: What is the difference between a partial DFA and a complete DFA?
defenseQuestions.answer: A partial DFA has missing transitions for certain state-symbol pairs, where unexpected inputs cause an undefined state or crash. A complete DFA defines δ for every pair in Q × Σ, mapping illegal inputs explicitly to an absorbing non-accepting TRAP state.
defenseQuestions.q: What is the difference between a partial DFA and a complete DFA?
defenseQuestions.a: A partial DFA has missing transitions for certain state-symbol pairs, where unexpected inputs cause an undefined state or crash. A complete DFA defines δ for every pair in Q × Σ, mapping illegal inputs explicitly to an absorbing non-accepting TRAP state.

slides.title: 06 // AUTOMATON SPECIFICATION: Formal 5-Tuple Definition
slides.category: FORMAL AUTOMATON DEFINITION: M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F)

presenter.name: Karthik Sai
presenter.topic: Chomsky Hierarchy, Kleene's Law, Total Completeness & 5-Tuple Definition

slides.spokenScript: Here we formalize the complete mathematical specification of our protocol inspector as a 5-tuple: M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F). Let us examine each component: Q is the set of 9 finite states: eight representing legal operational protocol conditions, plus one dedicated absorbing TRAP sink state. Σ is the input alphabet of 13 discrete symbols, abstracting HTTP network events. δ is the transition function, mapping Q cross Σ to Q across our 117-cell matrix. q₀ is the initial state, designated as IDLE, representing an uninitialized network connection. And F is the set of accepting states, which is the singleton set containing exclusively the CLOSED state. A network session is accepted if and only if it terminates gracefully in CLOSED.

defenseQuestions.answer: In formal protocol verification, a session is only fully compliant if it gracefully executes teardown. Intermediate states like RESPONSE_SENT represent active connections, not completed conversations.

slides.title: 07 // STATE REGISTER TAXONOMY: State Space Q & Accepting Boundary

presenter.name: Karthik Sai
presenter.topic: Chomsky Hierarchy, Kleene's Law, Total Completeness & 5-Tuple Definition

slides.spokenScript: To understand the topology of our state space Q, we partition the 9 states into three functional operational tiers: First, Handshake & Entry: beginning at initial state IDLE, transitioning to CONNECTED upon successful TCP synchronization. Second, Auth & Dispatch: encompassing REQUEST_RECEIVED, AUTH_CHECKED, AUTH_FAILED, RESPONSE_SENT, and ERROR—modeling the full operational request-response lifecycle. And third, Terminal Boundaries: On the legal side, we have CLOSED in F, representing graceful connection teardown. This is our sole accepting state. On the violation side, we have TRAP not in F. TRAP is an absorbing dead-end state: once entered, all 13 transitions loop indefinitely back into TRAP. An attacker cannot escape TRAP by sending subsequent valid packets. To detail our 13-symbol event alphabet and walk you through our graph topology and empirical trace proofs, I now invite Ojas Mohbansi to the podium.

slides.title: 08 // INPUT ALPHABET Σ (|Σ| = 13): 13-Symbol Protocol Event Alphabet

presenter.name: Ojas Mohbansi
presenter.topic: 13-Symbol Alphabet, 9-State Graph, 117-Cell Matrix & Trace Proofs (w1/w2)

slides.spokenScript: Thank you, Karthik. Respected members of the evaluation committee, my name is Ojas Mohbansi. I will present the Input Alphabet, the State Graph Topology, and our Formal Trace Verification Proofs. In formal language theory, an automaton requires an alphabet Σ. In TraceGuard AI, our pre-processing pipeline translates raw network packets into a discrete, well-defined 13-symbol alphabet grouped into four functional categories: First, Session Controls: CONNECT, CLOSE, and TIMEOUT—governing TCP session boundaries. Second, Authentication & Request: REQUEST, AUTH_SUCCESS, and AUTH_FAILURE—tracking client intent and credential verification. Third, Status Responses: RESPONSE_200, RESPONSE_301, and RESP_401_403—modeling standard HTTP server replies. And fourth, Faults & Violations: RESPONSE_500, MALFORMED, and ERROR_RESPONSE—capturing protocol corruption and server faults. Every observable packet is deterministically abstracted into exactly one of these 13 symbols.

presenter.name: Ojas Mohbansi
presenter.topic: 13-Symbol Alphabet, 9-State Graph, 117-Cell Matrix & Trace Proofs (w1/w2)

slides.spokenScript: This slide displays the complete directed transition graph of our 9-state automaton. Any protocol action that violates sequential grammar immediately routes into TRAP, where a self-loop traps the adversary indefinitely.

slides.title: 12 // ADVERSARIAL TRACE w₂: Out-of-Order Exploit Rejection

presenter.name: Ojas Mohbansi
presenter.topic: 13-Symbol Alphabet, 9-State Graph, 117-Cell Matrix & Trace Proofs (w1/w2)

slides.spokenScript: Now let us examine an active attack: adversarial trace w₂, representing an out-of-order execution exploit. Step 1: The attacker initiates a connection with CONNECT. The automaton enters CONNECTED. Step 2: Suddenly, before sending any REQUEST or completing authentication, the server or an adversary injects RESPONSE_200. In a stateless firewall, this packet looks harmless—it is a valid HTTP 200 payload. But in TraceGuard AI, our total transition matrix evaluates δ(CONNECTED, RESPONSE_200). Because receiving a response without a request violates protocol causality, this transition maps strictly to TRAP. Step 3 and 4: Even if the attacker subsequently sends legitimate REQUEST and CLOSE packets, the absorbing property of TRAP ensures that δ(TRAP, σ) = TRAP. The trace halts in TRAP not in F. The verdict is: REJECTED (w₂ not in L(M)). We have not merely flagged an anomaly; we have established a deterministic causal proof of an exploit. To formalize this trace classification mathematically and present our system architecture and machine learning pipeline, I now hand over the presentation to Darpan Jain.

slides.title: 13 // EXTENDED TRANSITION δ*(q₀, w): Three-Way Language Classification

presenter.name: Darpan Jain
presenter.topic: Three-Way Classification (δ*), Triad System Pipeline & Isolation Forest ML

slides.spokenScript: Thank you, Ojas. Respected professors and members of the examination committee, my name is Darpan Jain. I will present our Extended Transition Function, the System Architecture, and the Machine Learning Anomaly Guard. In formal language theory, an automaton processes strings of arbitrary length through the Extended Transition Function, denoted δ*. Defined inductively: The base case on the empty string ε is δ*(q, ε) = q. For any string w and symbol a, δ*(q, wa) = δ(δ*(q, w), a). In real-world network monitoring, an ongoing connection is not simply accepted or rejected at any random moment. TraceGuard AI operationalizes δ* into a Three-Way Language Classification: Category 1: ACCEPTED—when δ*(q₀, w) belongs to F. The session has executed legally and completed a graceful teardown in CLOSED. Category 2: INCOMPLETE VALID PREFIX—when δ*(q₀, w) is not in F union {TRAP}. The session is actively in progress; all transitions so far have been legal, but it has not yet reached the closing boundary. And Category 3: REJECTED—when δ*(q₀, w) equals TRAP. The sequence has violated protocol grammar and is permanently contained.

slides.title: 15 // STATISTICAL ANOMALY GUARD: Unsupervised Isolation Forest ML

presenter.name: Darpan Jain
presenter.topic: Three-Way Classification (δ*), Triad System Pipeline & Isolation Forest ML

slides.spokenScript: Now let us examine the statistical machine learning tier: the Unsupervised Isolation Forest. Why did we select an Isolation Forest rather than a supervised neural network? Because modern networks exhibit zero-day attacks with no prior training labels. Isolation Forest operates entirely unsupervised based on a geometric insight: anomalous data points are few and different, meaning they are isolated in fewer random partitioning splits than normal clusters. Our engine extracts 15 numerical session features, spanning: Volumetric metrics: packet counts, total bytes transferred, and average payload size; Temporal dynamics: overall session duration and inter-packet arrival variance; and Error profiles: HTTP error response ratios and authentication failure frequencies. The anomaly score s(x,n) is computed as 2 to the power of negative E(h(x)) over c(n), where E(h(x)) is the average path depth across our ensemble of isolation trees, and c(n) is the average path depth of an unsuccessful search in a Binary Search Tree. When volumetric floods or brute-force spikes occur, their path depths are significantly shorter, driving the score towards 1.0. To explain how our Consensus Arbiter combines these ML scores with our deterministic FSM proofs, I now invite Panda to the podium.

I will conclude our presentation by covering Hybrid Consensus Arbitration, our Live Demonstration Laboratory, our Chomsky Roadmap, and our Final Academic Conclusions. When combining deterministic logic with statistical machine learning, a critical architectural question arises: How do we resolve conflicting signals? If an attacker crafts an exploit that subtly violates protocol sequence order but closely mimics normal traffic volume, a naive average might allow the statistical model to suppress the alarm. TraceGuard AI solves this through our Weighted Consensus Formula with a Mandatory 60% Risk Floor: S_h = 0.6 times S_FSM plus 0.4 times S_ML. We assign 60% weight to formal protocol proof and 40% weight to statistical outlier probability. Crucially, we enforce our Risk Floor Invariant: If the DFA transitions into TRAP, S_FSM is immediately set to 1.0. Even if the Isolation Forest evaluates S_ML = 0.0, the resulting hybrid score is mathematically guaranteed to be at least 0.60—triggering an immediate, non-negotiable High-Severity incident. As our benchmark table shows: Pure ML suffers from high false alarms; signature engines like Snort cannot verify state sequences; TraceGuard AI delivers sub-millisecond latency, zero false positives on compliant grammar, and total explainability.

slides.title: 18 // CRITICAL EVALUATION & ROADMAP: Scope Limits & Chomsky Ascent

presenter.name: Panda
presenter.topic: Consensus Scoring (60% Floor), Live Automata Lab, Chomsky Ascent & Q.E.D.

slides.spokenScript: True academic rigor requires recognizing the boundary limits of one's current model. In our current implementation, TraceGuard AI operates on abstracted HTTP session event streams and synthetic benchmark corpora, demonstrating proof-of-concept correctness without parsing raw Layer-2 bitstreams. To push formal automata theory further into enterprise network security, we propose an Upward Chomsky Ascent: First, Ascending to Pushdown Automata (Type-2): regular languages cannot count unbounded matching pairs. By incorporating a stack automaton, we can recognize context-free languages of the form aⁿbⁿ, enabling the validation of deeply nested JSON objects, XML tags, and recursive RPC payload delimiters. Second, Product Automata for Concurrent Streams: modern protocols like HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 multiplex hundreds of concurrent bidirectional streams over a single connection. By constructing the tensor product of multiple DFAs, we can model asynchronous interleaving without state explosion. And third, Multi-Protocol Automata: extending our 5-tuple formulation to model TLS 1.3 cryptographic handshakes and SSH key exchanges.
